To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Children growing up in more economically deprived families made significantly more inhibitory control mistakes than their peers from families with more economic resources.

1) children from low-income families have lower inhibitory control ability at age 5 than their more advantaged peers, 2) this difference is not explained by child gender and 3) this difference in inhibitory control ability is not explained by differences in the rate of development of inhibitory ability between low-income children and their more advantaged counterparts.
(1) Children living in more economically deprived families have delayed development of inhibitory skills and (2) The impact of economic deprivation occurs before the age of 6 years.

how early economic deprivation affects the development of inhibitory processes in young children.

economic deprivation is related to early deficits in inhibitory control and that these early deficits are not overcome as children age, but instead persist into middle childhood, putting children on a developmental lag.

economic deprivation in early childhood may have lasting consequences on children's neurocognitive development.
